nodes.label: Yazdegerd III dies at Merv
nodes.full: Defeated at Nihavand in 642 — a rout Arab tradition itself called 'the Victory of Victories' — the last Sasanian king spent his final years as a fugitive across the Iranian plateau before being killed near Merv in 651, an inglorious end that nonetheless marked the real close of four centuries of Sasanian rule.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on the Battle of Nihavand and Yazdegerd's death.

nodes.label: Early governors
nodes.full: Abd Allah ibn Amir's forces pursued the fugitive last Sasanian king Yazdegerd III into Khorasan, where he was killed at Merv in 651 — nominally ending four centuries of Sasanian rule, though real Arab control over the plateau's interior remained thin and contested for decades afterward.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on the death of Yazdegerd III and the early Khorasan governorships.

nodes.label: Conquest of Khorasan
nodes.full: Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays led the Arab armies that secured Nishapur, Herat and Merv in a rapid campaign following Yazdegerd's death — though much of the interior plateau accepted tribute-paying submission rather than direct occupation, leaving Arab control genuinely thin outside the garrison towns for a generation.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on al-Ahnaf ibn Qays's Khorasan campaign.

nodes.label: Arab-Sasanian coinage
nodes.full: For decades after the conquest, mints across Khorasan and the plateau struck silver drachms carrying the Sasanian king's portrait and Zoroastrian fire-altar reverse largely unchanged, with only a brief Arabic religious phrase added to the margin — a numismatic continuity that outlasted the dynasty whose coinage it copied by nearly half a century.
nodes.src: Arab-Sasanian coin series, British Museum; Michael Bates, 'The Coinage of Syria under the Umayyads' and comparative eastern issues.

nodes.label: Abbasid-style dirham reaches east
nodes.full: Abd al-Malik's aniconic coinage reform of the 690s eventually displaced the Sasanian-style Arab-Sasanian drachms still being struck in Khorasan decades after the conquest, replacing royal portraiture and fire altars with purely epigraphic Islamic coin designs — the final numismatic break with the Sasanian past, arriving in the east well after it had reached the Arab heartlands.
nodes.src: Michael Bates, on the spread of Abd al-Malik's reformed coinage to the eastern provinces.

nodes.label: Dehqans keep the land
nodes.full: Many of the local Iranian landed gentry (dehqans) who had administered Sasanian rural estates kept their land and local authority by submitting and, over time, converting — a substantial continuity of the old agrarian elite beneath a changed political and religious order, rather than a wholesale replacement by Arab settlers.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, on dehqan submission agreements across the plateau.

nodes.label: Arabisation of the diwan
nodes.full: Provincial administration in Khorasan continued to run in Middle Persian under the existing Sasanian-trained bureaucratic class for decades after the conquest, before the diwan's records were converted to Arabic — a slower and later transition than in the Arab heartlands, reflecting how much the new regime still depended on inherited Sasanian administrative expertise.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, on the diwan's language conversion in the eastern provinces.

nodes.label: Qanats persist
nodes.full: The underground qanat networks that had underwritten plateau agriculture for over a millennium continued in operation through the conquest and the political upheavals that followed, their maintenance falling to local landholders and village communities largely independent of whichever distant power claimed sovereignty over the province.
nodes.src: Qanat survey evidence, Fars and Khorasan provinces; continuity inferred from unbroken settlement patterns.

nodes.label: Qutayba and Transoxiana
nodes.full: Governing Khorasan for a decade, Qutayba pushed the frontier of Muslim rule far beyond Iran itself into Transoxiana, taking Bukhara, Samarkand and Khwarazm — campaigns that used Khorasan's garrison as the launching point for the deepest Arab conquests into Central Asia.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Qutayba's Transoxianan campaigns.

nodes.label: Campaigns beyond the Oxus
nodes.full: Qutayba ibn Muslim's decade of campaigning took Bukhara, Samarkand and Khwarazm, using Khorasan's Arab and mawali garrison troops as the spearhead for conquests that extended Muslim rule deep into Central Asia beyond Iran's own eastern frontier.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Qutayba's campaigns.

nodes.label: Jizya and the mawali grievance
nodes.full: Umayyad governors in Khorasan continued taxing many Persian converts to Islam (mawali) as though they remained non-Muslim, denying them the fiscal relief conversion was supposed to bring — a concrete grievance that fed directly into the mawali support base Abu Muslim's revolutionary movement would later organise.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on mawali taxation grievances under Umayyad governors.

nodes.label: Mawali legal category
nodes.full: Non-Arab converts to Islam (mawali) occupied an ambiguous new legal status — nominally equal believers, but in practice often still taxed as non-Muslims and excluded from the stipends and status Arab Muslims enjoyed — a categorical grievance specific to the conquest generation that Abu Muslim's movement organised into a revolutionary constituency.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on mawali status and grievances under Umayyad rule.

nodes.label: Nasr ibn Sayyar
nodes.full: Nasr governed a Khorasan riven by Arab tribal factionalism and mounting Abbasid clandestine agitation among the mawali; his failure to suppress Abu Muslim's rising in time cost him the province, and he died a fugitive in 748 as the revolution he could not contain swept past him.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Nasr ibn Sayyar's governorship and flight.

nodes.label: Abu Muslim
nodes.full: A figure of obscure origins organised the Abbasid movement's clandestine network among Khorasan's mawali and Arab settlers alike, raised the black banners at Merv in 747, and led the army that destroyed the Umayyad Caliphate within three years — before the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, fearing his power, had him executed in 755.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Abu Muslim's rise, revolution and execution.

nodes.label: Bihafarid revolt
nodes.full: Bihafarid preached a syncretic doctrine blending Zoroastrian and Islamic elements and gathered a substantial following in rural Khorasan before Abu Muslim — himself just beginning his own rising — had him suppressed and killed, an early sign of the religious ferment the conquest had unsettled rather than resolved.
nodes.src: al-Biruni, The Chronology of Ancient Nations, on Bihafarid's movement.

nodes.label: March to the Zab
nodes.full: Abu Muslim's Khorasan-raised army swept west, defeating Umayyad forces repeatedly before the decisive Battle of the Great Zab in 750 destroyed the last Umayyad field army and opened the way to Damascus — a revolution launched from Khorasan that ended by installing an entirely new caliphal dynasty.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on the Battle of the Zab.

nodes.label: Execution and Sunpadh revolt
nodes.full: Abu Muslim's execution by the caliph he had made triggered Sunpadh's revolt in Khorasan, a rising that combined vengeance for Abu Muslim with an explicitly Zoroastrian-inflected, anti-Arab religious programme — proof that the conquest's political and religious settlement remained genuinely unstable a full century after Nihavand.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Sunpadh's revolt.

nodes.label: Papermaking via Talas
nodes.full: An Abbasid army built substantially around Khorasani troops defeated a Tang Chinese force at Talas in 751; Chinese papermakers among the prisoners are traditionally credited with introducing paper production to Samarkand shortly afterward — technology transfer riding directly on the same Khorasan-based military network that had carried the Abbasid revolution westward four years earlier.
nodes.src: al-Tha'alibi, Yatimat al-Dahr (11th c., recording the Talas paper-making tradition); Jonathan Bloom, Paper before Print (2001), assessing the tradition's reliability.

nodes.label: Paper spreads west
nodes.full: From Samarkand's new paper mills, the technology spread west through Khorasan to Baghdad within a few decades — paper's cheapness compared to parchment and papyrus directly enabled the explosive growth of Abbasid administrative record-keeping and, in time, the great translation movement's output.
nodes.src: Jonathan Bloom, Paper before Print: The History and Impact of Paper in the Islamic World (2001).

nodes.label: Barmakid Buddhist origins
nodes.full: Before their conversion to Islam and rise as Abbasid administrators, the Barmakid family hereditarily administered the Nawbahar Buddhist monastery at Balkh, described in detail by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang decades before the conquest — a reminder that eastern Khorasan's religious landscape included a substantial Buddhist presence alongside Zoroastrianism.
nodes.src: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, on the Nawbahar monastery at Balkh.

nodes.label: Barmakid governors
nodes.full: Descended from a family of hereditary administrators of a Buddhist monastery at Balkh, the Barmakids rose to govern Khorasan and then to dominate the Abbasid vizierate at Baghdad itself for a generation, before Harun al-Rashid abruptly and violently purged the family from power in 803.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings; Ibn Khallikan, Wafayat al-A'yan, on the Barmakid family.

nodes.label: Tahir ibn Husayn
nodes.full: Tahir ibn Husayn, the general whose army had won the caliph al-Ma'mun's civil war against his brother al-Amin, was rewarded with the governorship of Khorasan in 821 — a post he and his heirs held in practice as hereditary rulers loyal to Baghdad only in name, the first quasi-independent Iranian dynasty since the Arab conquest.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Tahir's appointment and the Fourth Fitna.

nodes.label: Tahir drops the caliph name
nodes.full: Tradition holds that Tahir ibn Husayn briefly omitted the Abbasid caliph's name from the Friday sermon at Nishapur in 821, a symbolic assertion of autonomy quickly walked back but long remembered as the moment Khorasan's governor first acted like something closer to a king than a provincial appointee.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on Tahir's governorship.

nodes.label: Khorasan the kingmaker
nodes.full: Khorasan's military and political weight decided two successive struggles for the caliphate itself — Abu Muslim's army installed the Abbasid dynasty in 750, and Tahir's army decided the Fourth Fitna for al-Ma'mun in 813 — a province that began the era as a distant conquest ended it as the power broker of the entire Muslim world.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, on the Fourth Fitna (809–813).

nodes.label: Empire ends, Muslim Iran forms
nodes.full: Between Yazdegerd III's death and Tahir's autonomous governorship lies not a single conquest but a century and a half of negotiated, uneven transformation — an empire's political end at Merv in 651 and a genuinely new religious and cultural order still only partially formed at Nishapur in 821.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History of Prophets and Kings, spanning the whole period.

nodes.label: Khwaday-Namag continues
nodes.full: The Sasanian royal chronicle tradition, the Khwaday-Namag ('Book of Lords'), continued to be copied and reworked in Middle Persian after the conquest before its eventual translation into Arabic — the direct ancestor, two centuries later, of Ferdowsi's Persian national epic the Shahnameh.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist (10th c.), listing Khwaday-Namag manuscripts and their translators.

nodes.label: Kalila wa Dimna translated
nodes.full: The Persian convert Ibn al-Muqaffa translated the Pahlavi version of the Indian fable collection Kalila wa Dimna into Arabic, transmitting a text that had itself already crossed from Sanskrit into Persian centuries earlier — a chain of translation spanning three languages that made him one of early Abbasid Iraq's most influential literary figures before his execution around 756–759 on suspicion of heresy.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist, on Ibn al-Muqaffa's translations and death.

nodes.label: Roots of the Shuubiyya
nodes.full: Persian secretaries and literary figures in Abbasid service began articulating an explicit defence of Persian cultural and administrative achievement against Arab claims of inherent superiority — the early current that would crystallise a century later into the full literary movement known as the Shu'ubiyya.
nodes.src: Ibn Qutayba, Kitab al-'Arab (written partly in response to these early Shu'ubi arguments).

nodes.label: Hanzala Badghisi
nodes.full: Writing in Badghis under the last Tahirid-era Khorasan, Hanzala is remembered by later Persian literary tradition as among the very first poets to compose in New Persian rather than Arabic — a single verse's survival marking the tentative beginning of the literary renaissance that would flower fully under the Samanids a century later.
nodes.src: Muhammad Awfi, Lubab al-Albab (13th c. anthology), preserving the tradition of Hanzala's verse.

nodes.label: The Khorasan highway
nodes.full: The great road linking Baghdad through Rayy, Nishapur and Merv to Transoxiana and onward toward China remained the empire's busiest eastern artery under Arab rule exactly as it had been under the Sasanians — political conquest changed who governed the route far more than it changed the route's own economic importance.
nodes.src: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (9th c., describing the road network he inherited).

nodes.label: Caravanserais
nodes.full: Way-stations and fortified caravanserais along the Khorasan highway, many built on or near earlier Sasanian road-station foundations, were maintained and expanded to support the growing volume of trade and official traffic between Baghdad and the eastern provinces.
nodes.src: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, on the road stations of the Khorasan route.

nodes.label: Khorasan hub to the east
nodes.full: Merv and Nishapur functioned as the last great entrepôts before the routes to Transoxiana, India and China, positioning Khorasan's merchants — Muslim, Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist alike — as the middlemen of an overland trade whose eastern half had barely noticed the change of political rule to its west.
nodes.src: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, on the eastward trade routes from Khorasan.

nodes.label: Zoroastrians as dhimmi
nodes.full: As protected non-Muslim subjects (dhimmi) paying the jizya, Zoroastrian communities kept fire temples operating across the plateau, including the great royal fire of Adur Gushnasp — legal toleration that preserved the religion as a substantial minority presence for centuries, even as the political order that had once sponsored it as a state cult was gone for good.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, on dhimmi status and the jizya in former Sasanian territory.

nodes.label: Zoroastrian family law
nodes.full: Zoroastrian communities retained the right to apply their own religious family law, including next-of-kin marriage practices Islamic law prohibited for Muslims — a specific legal accommodation of dhimmi communal autonomy that let Zoroastrian religious practice continue on its own terms even as the community's overall size and standing steadily diminished.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, on dhimmi communal legal autonomy.

nodes.label: Zoroastrian textual transmission
nodes.full: Zoroastrian priests continued copying and orally transmitting Avestan and Pahlavi religious literature under Muslim rule, laying the groundwork for the major compilations — above all the Denkard — that later Zoroastrian scholars would complete once the religion's minority status made textual preservation an urgent priority rather than an assumed continuity.
nodes.src: Denkard, Book 3 (compiled later, describing the transmission effort as an ongoing, multi-generational project).

nodes.label: Slow pace of conversion
nodes.full: Conversion to Islam across the Iranian plateau proceeded far more gradually than in Arabia or Iraq — modern demographic analysis of conversion narratives suggests a Muslim majority was not reached in most of Iran until roughly a century or more after this folio's own end, a slower and more negotiated religious transformation than the conquest narrative alone would suggest.
nodes.src: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period: An Essay in Quantitative History (1979), on Iranian conversion curves.

nodes.label: Abd al-Malik reforms coinage
nodes.full: The caliph aniconic coinage reform of the 690s replaced portraits and fire altars with epigraphic designs across the empire.
nodes.src: background — see the Caliphate 632–750 folio

nodes.label: Fourth Fitna
nodes.full: The civil war between al-Amin and al-Ma’mun, decided by the army of Tahir ibn Husayn, is the context for Tahir’s reward.
nodes.src: named in this folio’s p6 and w2; see the Caliphate 750–945 folio
